Deadly earthquake in Colombia hits Manizales, damaging cathedral and homes Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 11/08/2026 - 12:09 GMT+2 Manizales, in Colombia’s western Caldas department, was among the areas hardest hit by Monday’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake, with streets littered with rubble as rescue teams searched damaged buildings for survivors. … More Footage from 10 August shows collapsed buildings and ambulances as residents make their way through areas closed off by authorities. One of the side towers of the city’s neo-Gothic Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary was also brought down by the force of the tremor, sending debris into the surrounding streets. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT At least two people were killed in Manizales, while dozens of homes and commercial buildings were destroyed or severely damaged. The mayor said more than a dozen commercial properties and over 20 homes had been partially or completely destroyed. Engineers were inspecting cracked facades and weakened structures to determine which buildings needed to be evacuated. The city activated an emergency command centre, opened temporary shelters and suspended classes in schools and universities. Flights at Manizales airport were halted while engineers checked the runways and terminal for damage, while the city's cable car service was also suspended pending safety inspections. A curfew was imposed to prevent looting and allow rescue and assessment work to continue. Firefighters and rescue teams remained on the ground as authorities warned that people could still be trapped beneath the rubble. The earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time on Monday, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó, around 400 kilometres west of Bogotá. The government declared a national disaster to speed up rescue operations and provide assistance to affected communities. Photograph: US navy/Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: US aircraft carrier arrives to relieve USS Lincoln amid reports of poor living conditions The USS George Washington has arrived in the Middle East. Plus, an investigation into the add-on utility fees that can lead to evictions Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Jem Bartholomew Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.08 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. The USS George Washington aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln from its record deployment, amid concerns about poor living conditions and morale. US Central Command announced on Thursday that the Washington arrived in the area on Wednesday, and posted an image of sailors working on the flight deck as the ship transited the Arabian Sea. According to the New York Times , which cited a US official, the Lincoln began its home journey to San Diego on Thursday. Recent reports have rung alarm bells about conditions on the Lincoln. “I just don’t really think they’re treating them like people. I think they’re treating them like a uniform, like a pawn on a chessboard,” the wife of a sailor onboard told the Guardian’s Anna Betts this week. What are conditions like on the Lincoln? The ship has spent more than 250 days at sea supporting US operations against Iran without a significant port visit or date to return home for the 5,000 sailors and marines onboard. Reports from families of crew members published in the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes military newspapers described food and water shortages, disrupted mail services, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. ‘It kept adding up’: Investigation reveals how add-on utility fees can lead to eviction for tenants View image in fullscreen Signs hung by members of Los Angeles’ Virgil Square Tenants Association protesting their complex’s utility billing practices. Composite: Virgil Square Tenants Association An investigation co-published by the Guardian and the Economic Hardship Reporting Project, a journalism non-profit that supports stories about inequality and poverty in the US, has revealed a problem emerging nationwide : fees charged on top of rent known as “ratio utility billing system” fees – or Rubs. Rubs, unlike standard utility bills, where tenants owe money to the utility company, are owed to the landlord and often paid through a third-party billing company. Many leases that include Rubs are written so tenants can be evicted for not paying utilities, even if they have paid their rent. For working-class and low-income tenants such as Constance Soule, an 81-year-old disabled Alzheimer’s patient, falling behind on these utility charges can lead to eviction notices, Tracie McMillan reports. “It just kept adding up,” Margot Jones, Soule’s sister, said. Tenants in Los Angeles and Seattle have launched “Rubs strikes”, refusing to pay utilities until landlords agree to reduce charges that can approach $300 a month per apartment. How are people fighting back? At least 13 lawsuits have challenged Rubs since the start of 2025 across five states – including a case in California that led to a nearly $500,000 settlement last fall with a national property manager. “Some California landlords have tried to get away with illegal rent increases by shifting utilities and other fees to tenants and pretending those new charges are not ‘rent’” under state law, Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said when announcing the settlement. Efforts to limit or ban add-on utility fees are also gaining momentum across several cities. In other news … View image in fullscreen A screengrab from social media of Itamar Ben-Gvir at a building site for gallows where Palestinian convicts will be executed. Photograph: X Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has been condemned for posting a gloating video of the construction of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – will be hanged. It comes after the minister sparked a backlash a few days ago for saying there should be “30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night” in Gaza. Progressive Aisha Wahab has been elected to Congress in a special election, following a bitter intraparty battle over the seat formerly held by Eric Swalwell. North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said . It comes after Donald Trump’s order earlier this week to scale back US military drills with South Korea. Fans’ groups worldwide have launched a petition calling for the resignation of Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, and for wholesale reform of soccer’s international governing organization. Stat of the day: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal View image in fullscreen A plane carrying the deportees from the US arrives at Roberts international airport, outside Monrovia, Liberia, on Thursday. Photograph: Alexander Wiaplah/AP Twenty deportees from the US arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement in which the west African country will receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah, said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean. Culture pick: It Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s best View image in fullscreen Akira Jackson in a scene from It Ends. Photograph: Neon/AP A crew of aimless twentysomethings take a late-night drive to get food, but their GPS leads them deeper and deeper into a desolate forest. “It Ends often reaches the quality of high-concept cult horror classics while also nodding to our uniquely modern malaise,” writes Owen Myers in his four-star review . Don’t miss this: How to get back into reading books – podcast View image in fullscreen The panelists suggest titles – from the Greek classics to ‘romantasy’ – that may help you kick the screen habit. Photograph: Westend61/Getty For Today in Focus, the Guardian convenes a specialist panel on which books may help you put your phone away and get reading again . “I think we’re all bored of talking about ChatGPT at parties, and really interested in getting back to things that feel human,” Rebecca Liu, acting Saturday culture editor and a Booker prize judge, says. Climate check: How one American couple ditched their lawn and created a wildlife haven – and you could too View image in fullscreen Fritz and McGuire’s garden is a thriving native ecosystem in the middle of the suburbs. Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian Novice gardeners James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz wanted to try something new when they moved from Chicago out to the suburb of Highland Park, Illinois. They set about rewilding their garden. “It brings us a lot of peace and tranquility in a very troubled world,” McGuire says. Read their story – and see tips for how to rewild a lawn . Last Thing: The Guardian reveals 2026’s Invertebrate of the year – the leaf sheep View image in fullscreen The leaf sheep feeds on algae that grow in fine silts around shallow reefs. Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/Alamy The winner of the global ballot for Invertebrate of the year has now been revealed: the leaf sheep ( Costasiella kuroshimae ) . The leaf sheep, which lives in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines and feeds on algae, has inspired at least one Pokémon character. https://www.theupcoming.co.uk/2026/08/18.text: Culture Food & Travel News & features Nakimushi to bring ramen bar and townhouse restaurant to Notting Hill this September Nakimushi to bring ramen bar and townhouse restaurant to Notting Hill this September 18 th August 2026 Food & Travel Desk Food & Travel Desk · 18 August 2026 A new three-storey Japanese restaurant will open in a listed Victorian townhouse in Notting Hill this September, bringing together two previously temporary projects – the Urchin counter and Robin’s Ramen – under one permanent roof. Nakimushi comes from the team behind the Michelin-starred Dorian, EEL Sushi, Supermarket of Dreams and the Notting Hill Fish+Meat Shop, and is led by joint head chefs Yuji Shimokawa Kelly and Robin Kosuge. The new venue works with a dual format: the ground floor houses a ramen bar built around an open kitchen with communal seating, serving Tokyo-style ramen alongside a short list of snacks and cold starters, while the first floor holds a 25-seat restaurant and bar with a broader contemporary Japanese menu. There’s also a top floor visible to guests that contains the chefs’ preparation kitchen and a state-of-the-art larder. The building has been restored with pale timber panelling, cabinetry and gridded ceilings, parquet flooring, satin-finished brass features and hand-glazed Japanese tiles in varying shades of oxblood – a colour repeated across all three floors. Guests enter beneath a custom-made noren curtain through an oxblood shopfront set against the original brick façade. Ground-floor dishes include a Lobster Ramen with Seafood Paitan and Komatsuna and Charshu Pork Belly Ramen made with Basque Chicken Broth and Ajitama . There are also cold plates such as Wild Hamachi with Yukari Ponzu and Nori Oil , a Namayasai Salad with shio dressing, and Corn Tempura with Fig Leaf Salt , served in an intentionally energetic atmosphere that recalls the back-street ramen shops of Tokyo. Meanwhile, on the first-floor there’s a steadier pace and a menu that extends to Red Prawn and Courgette Gyoza with Umeboshi , Quail Tempura with Jerk Tendashi and Apricot Purée and Chicken Karaage with Chive Oroshi and Ponzu. Larger sharing plates come in the form of Steamed Turbot with Red Vinegar An , Grilled Ibérico x Duroc Pork Loin with Red Almond Miso and Grilled Tuna Kama with Padrón Pepper Dashi and Kimizu . Ramen also features, as a consistent thread across the venue. Behind the bar, the cocktail list is built around Japanese spirits and ingredients, including shochu highballs in full and low-alcohol versions: the Midori-Hai (shochu, Midori, miso sherry and shiso) and the Hato-Hai , named after the Japanese word for dove, which is a shochu version of a Paloma made with maraschino and grapefruit. Sakes and unpasteurised nama sakes feature, with aged examples served by the glass, among them Shirayuki Edo Genroku (a Junmai brewed by Konishi Shuzo to a recipe dating from 1703) and Hayashi Honten Golden Amber (a 12-year-old Junmai Koshu). The wine list focuses on Burgundy and Italian bottles. Shimokawa Kelly, who is Japanese-British and grew up in London, began his career with the opening team at Dinings SW3 before working in Japan and then spending four years at the two-Michelin-starred Umu in Mayfair. He met the entrepreneur Chris D’Sylva and Kosuge during lockdown at the Notting Hill Fish+Meat Shop, later joining Dorian and contributing to its first star. He subsequently opened Urchin, which began as a ten-seat counter in Sifnos, Greece, before running as a 12-month pop-up at Supermarket of Dreams in Holland Park. Kosuge was born in London to a Polish mother and Japanese father. He trained in pastry at Kouzu in Belgravia, Selfridges and a Paris boulangerie before spending two years with Dominique Ansel in Tokyo. Returning to London in 2019, he expanded his expertise to sushi at the Notting Hill Fish+Meat Shop, and joined the opening team at Dorian in 2022. Robin’s Ramen began as a one-day pop-up at EEL Sushi in summer 2025 and became an eight-month residency at Supermarket of Dreams from October 2025 until May 2026. The two distinct yet complementary experiences at Nakimushi, like the two lead chefs, are united by a shared commitment to exceptional produce and traditional Japanese techniques. Bookings are open now. Food Desk Nakimushi opens on 7 th September 2026 at 7 Kensington Mall, London W8 4EB. For further information or to book a table, visit the restaurant’s website here. https://www.dw.com/en/us-court-rejects-t.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mt4l The second Trump administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to 3rd countries [FILE: August 27, 2026] Image: Ketlain Difficile/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A US federal appeals court has largely upheld a ruling blocking the Trump administration from rapidly deporting migrants to third countries without giving them a meaningful chance to raise safety concerns. The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston said Friday that migrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture there. What did the court say about the DHS policy? The case challenges a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy allowing migrants with final deportation orders to be sent to countries other than their own, provided authorities have diplomatic assurances they will not face persecution or torture. The court said the policy could deny protections to migrants sent to unfamiliar countries without notice. The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court. DHS General Counsel James Percival said on X that the policy remains in force because Friday's ruling has not yet taken effect. "If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," Percival wrote. The order comes as two men deported by the US to Equatorial Guinea were arbitrarily detained, with police covering their heads with bags, beating them and holding them at gunpoint in a hotel turned into a detention center, the AP reported. More than 25,000 deported to third countries Since US President Donald Trump returned to office, his administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First. Some of the third countries immigrants are being deported to are: South Sudan Eswatini Uganda Equatorial Guinea Liberia Central African Republic The third-country deals have drawn criticism from human rights groups, as several participating nations have notoriously repressive governments and poor human rights records . https://www.theguardian.com/world/video/.text: 1:44 France Police and protesters exchange teargas and fireworks in demonstrations across France – video Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday amid fresh demonstrations over school funding and the cost of living. A peaceful protest during the day in Paris – with at least 110,000 people marching along the eastern edge of the city – descended into violent clashes with police by the time night fell. Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and the other in Toulouse.
